stories.headline: Artificial Analysis ranks frontier models by how well they drive a robot arm
stories.standfirst: Its AA-Robotics v0.1 preview gives each model a six-axis arm and four cameras, and the top score is 69 for GPT-6 Astra, at about 30 minutes a task.
body: Artificial Analysis, the firm that benchmarks AI models, launched AA-Robotics v0.1 on Wednesday. It describes the research preview as a test of how well frontier language models understand the physical world, plan and act in it. Each model controls a six-axis robot arm with a simple objective, and the firm released results for its first eight tasks, covering control and dexterity, spatial reasoning and adaptability.

Per the firm's thread, models get only brief instructions: how to reach the arm over a simple HTTP API, which arm it is and how to submit an attempt. The arm is a Hiwonder NexArm, with no further specifications given. Models see the table through four cameras, three around it and one on the wrist, and write and run code to plan movements. Attempts are zero-shot, and a pass scores 100.

Artificial Analysis says GPT-6 Astra places first with 69, ahead of GPT-6.1 Sol at 65 and Gemini 4 Argon at 55. Claude Opus 5.5 scores 49 and Claude Fable 5.1 scores 46. The firm says GPT-6.1 Sol is the cheapest at $1.93 a task on average, while GPT-6 Astra costs $16.36, more than eight times as much, for four extra points.

Speed is the weak spot. The firm says models take about 30 minutes on average to finish each tabletop task, and that the best are roughly 100 times slower and 10 times more expensive than a human. It calls them far too slow and expensive for production use, though it expects that to change quickly. That is the firm's own reading of its own test.

It lists three kinds of mistake. Models miss grasps and placements, which drops objects or pushes them out of reach. They reason poorly about space, which leads to the wrong sequence and knocked-over towers. And they misjudge success, often carrying on after a task has passed. The scores are Artificial Analysis's alone, and no outside group has reproduced them.

stories.headline: Nvidia opens a 120B vision model and a 24GB Bolt for desktops
stories.standfirst: Nvidia says its open Nemotron 3.5 Super VL has 120 billion parameters, 12 billion active, and Artificial Analysis rates it the top US open-weight model at 26.5, ahead of a 24GB Bolt for RTX laptops.
body: Nvidia released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on Thursday, an open model with 120 billion parameters of which 12 billion are active per token. The company says it reads documents, charts, tables, web pages and video, calls tools, and is built for always-on agents. Weights are on Hugging Face, OpenRouter and ModelScope, and the model is packaged for Nvidia's NIM service.

Nvidia makes the performance claims. Its blog says the model matches Nvidia's largest reasoning model on multimodal agentic tasks at about one-fifth the parameter count. It also calls the model the fastest open agentic model in its class, roughly five times quicker than the next best. Nvidia says it trained on about 26 trillion tokens. The blog names no licence, only open weights, datasets and training recipes.

Artificial Analysis, which runs its own tests, scored the model 26.5 on its Intelligence Index. That makes it the leading US open-weight model, the firm says, edging out Thinking Machines' Inkling Small at 25.7. It reports the score is twice that of the earlier Nemotron 3 Super at 13, while using about 60 percent fewer output tokens per task.

The smaller release is the one people can run at home. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B uses native 2-bit quantisation to fit in 24GB of memory, Nvidia says, and works with llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, Unsloth and vLLM. Artificial Analysis gives it 21 on its index. A 4GB Bolt E4B follows on 23 October.

LM Studio says Super VL is already available in its app and needs about 70GB of RAM to run locally. Nvidia says Bolt is built for its RTX Spark laptops, which arrive on 16 October. Scale AI, AfterQuery, AI21 and Mercor are among the firms Nvidia says are customising the model, and no outside testing beyond Artificial Analysis has been published yet.

stories.headline: Black Forest Labs' FLUX.3 Klein draws to a box layout in 2 seconds
stories.standfirst: Hugging Face says FLUX.3 Image Klein makes a 1024-pixel image in about two seconds on an H100 and lets users draw boxes to set the layout.
body: Black Forest Labs' FLUX.3 Image Klein reached Hugging Face's Diffusers library on Thursday, and image host fal added it the same day. Hugging Face's launch post describes two checkpoints. Klein is distilled to run 16 steps with no guidance, and Klein Base takes 50 steps and is the one meant for fine-tuning.

The headline feature is layout control. Users supply JSON bounding boxes on a 0 to 1000 scale, and the model places content inside them. It also accepts several reference images, addressed as numbered tags, for editing and style transfer, and renders text. fal's post says you draw a box and get exactly that layout.

Hugging Face reports its own timings on one H100 80GB, averaged over three runs: 1.93 seconds for a 1024-pixel text-to-image, 3.87 seconds with one reference image and 4.10 seconds for a layout edit. Peak memory was 18.8 GiB after loading in bf16, 14.35 GiB in fp8 and 13.4 GiB in nvfp4 on an RTX 6000.

The post does not reconcile the model's size. Its model pages list 6B parameters, while a Spaces card says 5.6B open weights, so the exact count is unclear. It also does not state the licence. The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, and Diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both generation and editing.

The numbers come from Hugging Face's own tests of the distilled checkpoint, and no independent benchmark of image quality has been published. The fp8 weights get fast kernels on Ada, Hopper and Blackwell cards, while older GPUs save memory but gain no speed, the post says. The nvfp4 version is fast only on Blackwell.

stories.headline: Krea opens its Krea 3 editing beta, promising 2K edits in 8 seconds
stories.standfirst: Krea says its new Krea 3 model makes end-to-end 2K image edits in under eight seconds and matches Nano Banana Pro quality, and the beta is open now.
body: Krea opened the beta of Krea 3 on Thursday, which it calls a new frontier for image editing. The company's announcement on X lists three claims: end-to-end 2K edits in under eight seconds, quality that matches Nano Banana Pro or GPT Image 2.5, and bounding-box control with precise multi-turn edits. A launch video is attached to the post.

Those figures are Krea's own, and no independent comparison has been published. The company pairs the announcement with two videos, one on how its research team built the model's visual intelligence and one on using it for fast iteration. Krea says speed matters most for creative workflows, where people try many variations before picking one.

Developer synthwavedd, who posted a hands-on take within minutes of the launch, says Krea 3 reaches Nano Banana Pro quality at four times the speed and a quarter of the cost. They describe giving it a character, a product shot or a pile of references and getting edits back in under eight seconds. That is one user's early impression, not a test.

Krea had announced Krea 3 in August as part of a push towards editing agents, according to coverage of that event. This release is the first time the model is open for people to try. Krea's post points to a page to learn more and get access, and the posts reviewed give no pricing or limits.

Nobody outside Krea has yet published side-by-side results against the models it names. The speed claim is also unqualified: Krea does not say which hardware or image sizes the eight-second figure covers.

stories.headline: Mistral's Timestral forecasting models start at 5 million parameters
stories.standfirst: Mistral says its first time-series family tops three zero-shot forecasting leaderboards with a 209M model, while the 5M version forecasts a day ahead in 10 milliseconds on a server CPU.
body: Mistral released Timestral on Thursday, its first family of time-series foundation models. There are four sizes, at 5 million, 28 million, 123 million and 209 million parameters, sharing one architecture and training recipe. A GitHub repository and a Hugging Face collection are linked from the announcement.

Mistral says the 209M model ranks first among pre-trained, zero-shot models on the GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench leaderboards, using two-thirds the parameters of the previous best and a single checkpoint with no ensembling. It also says the 28M model beats Chronos-2, which is about four times larger, on GIFT-Eval and TIME.

Speed is the other claim. On an 8-thread server CPU, Mistral says one-day-ahead forecasts from three weeks of 15-minute history take 10 milliseconds with the 5M model and 140 milliseconds with the 209M. Forecasts are probabilistic and multivariate, return 21 quantiles, and can take past-only and known-future covariates over a 32,768-step context.

Mistral says it trained mostly on synthetic data, then post-trained on a mix of real and synthetic series. The weights are released under what it calls a Modified MIT licence, and it offers on-premises, private-cloud and air-gapped deployment, plus fine-tuning through its Forge service. The page does not spell out the licence's modifications.

The benchmark results are Mistral's own, and a technical report with full numbers is still to come. No outside group has reproduced the leaderboard placings yet. Mistral has not yet said when the report will appear.

stories.headline: Google's Universal Cart reaches Search and Gemini for US shoppers
stories.standfirst: Google says its Universal Cart now saves products from any retailer, watches for price drops and restocks, and checks out through its open Universal Commerce Protocol.
body: Google's Universal Cart is rolling out across Google Search and the Gemini app in the US, the company announced on Thursday. It first previewed the tool at its I/O event in May. The Verge, TechCrunch and 9to5Google all reported the launch, which arrives ahead of the holiday shopping season.

The cart holds items from multiple retailers in one place and keeps their progress when users return later, TechCrunch reported. Google says it can send an alert when a saved item drops in price or when an out-of-stock product returns. It can also factor in credit-card perks when suggesting how to pay.

Google says the cart surfaces relevant promo codes as well. Checkout runs on the Universal Commerce Protocol, an open standard Google introduced earlier this year to let AI agents and retailers work together, including at checkout. Google has not said in the coverage reviewed which retailers are signed up to it.

The cart joins two other shopping tools Google already offers: conversational product discovery in AI Mode, and Let Google Call, which uses an AI agent to check stock at nearby stores. TechCrunch notes that Amazon, OpenAI and other rivals have also added agentic shopping features this year.

The rollout is US-only, and Google has given no date for other countries. The claims about price tracking and checkout come from Google. The outlets reporting the launch describe the features from the company's announcement and have not published hands-on tests of how reliably alerts or checkout work.

stories.headline: Simons Foundation, OpenAI and Anthropic fund a $15M AI-for-maths effort
stories.standfirst: The Simons Foundation says it will run a $15 million open call to help mathematicians check AI-produced results, with OpenAI putting in $5 million and both labs supplying compute.
body: The Simons Foundation announced on Thursday a $15 million initiative to help mathematicians make sense of results produced by AI. The foundation says the money comes from itself, Anthropic and OpenAI together, and that the foundation will manage and award it, including through an open call for proposals.

OpenAI said on X that it is contributing $5 million. In its post, the company said it wants to support the mathematics community in turning AI progress into deeper human understanding, and that the money covers workshops, conferences and special programmes. OpenAI mentioned results it recently published, without detailing them in the post.

According to the foundation, the funding could help researchers evaluate recent AI-assisted results, learn the new tools, share perspectives and shape collective standards for using AI. Anthropic and OpenAI will also give researchers the foundation supports access to AI tools and computing resources, and the foundation says this extends beyond mathematics to basic science.

Foundation president David Spergel said the community should be driving discussions of how these tools are evaluated, rather than any single company or institution. The foundation points to its earlier funding of the Lean proof assistant, which it says made AI-assisted proofs possible and changed how mathematicians work.

The announcement does not say how many grants will be made or when the call opens, and the funding may not all be new money. Anthropic's share and the foundation's own are not stated in the sources reviewed. The post drew 64 points on Hacker News within about an hour.

stories.headline: GPT-6-Astra solves 49 of 50 physics research problems in a new test
stories.standfirst: A 35-author benchmark says OpenAI's GPT-6-Astra in Codex got 49 of 50 theoretical physics problems right at under $3 each, while Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code scored 92 percent.
body: GPT-6-Astra answered 49 of 50 theoretical physics research problems correctly in a new benchmark called TheoPhysEval, The Decoder reported on Thursday. Thirty-five researchers from institutions including Harvard, KU Leuven, the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences and Google DeepMind built the test. Astra ran inside OpenAI's Codex, averaged under $3 a problem and cost just under $116 in total.

The problems are unpublished, span eleven subfields and have verifiable answers. The authors call them turn-the-crank tasks: known methods applied to slightly altered questions, often made by changing values in the contributors' own recent papers. A leading expert would need about a day per problem, they say. Agents got no human hints and ran twice, once with web search and once offline.

Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code scored 92 percent, according to The Decoder's account. Gemini 3.8 Flash reached 68 percent, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 54 percent and GLM 5.3 42 percent. Without web search, Astra and Opus both scored 92 percent. With search, Astra missed only one problem, and that one stumped every model tested.

The authors flag limits. Follow-ups with experts found small errors in some reference answers, and Astra was correct every time once they were fixed, which may explain why agents score higher here than on other physics benchmarks. Web access changed little, which the authors read as a sign models have largely memorised the literature.

The authors say the benchmark covers routine research work, not open major questions, and that agents lack research taste, struggling to pick promising related problems. Their observations cannot be quantified, they write, and are not a forecast. The problems and test setup are available as a dataset on Hugging Face. The Decoder is the only outlet reviewed that reports the results.

stories.headline: StepFun opens weights for 600B-parameter Step 5 Preview
stories.standfirst: StepFun says its agent-focused Step 5 Preview, a 600B mixture-of-experts model with a 1M-token window, is downloadable now, with vLLM and SGLang support from day one.
body: StepFun, the Chinese lab, said on X on Thursday that Step 5 Preview is now open weights, with BF16 and FP8 checkpoints on Hugging Face and ModelScope alongside a technical blog. The company describes it as a sparse mixture-of-experts model with 600 billion parameters in total and 27 billion active for each token.

According to StepFun, the model takes text and images, handles up to one million tokens of input and output combined, and is built for long-horizon agentic work: coding, software engineering, professional knowledge work and finance. Adina Yakup, posting on X, called finance a strong focus and the licence customised.

The model card names the licence StepFun Model License 1.0, which it describes as Apache-2.0-style with extra attribution and commercial-licence conditions. Its benchmark results appear only in a chart image, citing GDPval-AA v2.1 scores from Artificial Analysis as of September 20 and DeepSWE v1.1. The text does not name the comparison models.

Both vLLM and SGLang said they support the model from day zero. The card lists FP8 serving on four B300 or eight H200 GPUs, and BF16 on eight B300 or sixteen H200. It says the full BF16 route through Transformers is not yet validated end to end. No independent tests had appeared when this was written, so the capability claims are StepFun's own.

stories.headline: Swiss Apertus 1.5 takes images and audio, with a 262,144-token window
stories.standfirst: The Swiss AI team's release notes describe 8B and 70B open models under Apache 2.0, trained on data it calls permissively licensed, while admitting they still trail frontier open weights.
body: The Swiss AI initiative published release notes on Hugging Face on Thursday for Apertus 1.5, a family of 8B and 70B models released under Apache 2.0. The notes say the weights have been available since July 24, and list base, SFT, RLVR and DPO checkpoints for both sizes in an Apertus v1.5 collection.

The team says continued pretraining added four trillion tokens to the 8B model and two trillion to the 70B, bringing the totals to 19 trillion and 17 trillion. The models accept text, images and audio but output text only. The notes call speech support experimental, and the context window is 262,144 tokens, four times that of Apertus 1.0.

The authors say all training data is publicly available and permissively licensed, with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. The post-training recipe includes about 3.7 million supervised samples and reinforcement learning on about 350,000 prompts. A final charter-alignment stage applies only to the 8B model.

On benchmarks, the notes say the 8B beats similar-sized open models on instruction following and multilingual tasks and matches GPT-OSS-20B on the Last Translation Benchmark. The post gives no scores in text, and the claims are the developers' own. They concede the models are still trailing frontier open-weight models, and announce a roughly 600B sparse Apertus 2.0 as a plan, not a release.

stories.headline: Amazon's Bee adds a $75 wristband and a phone-back recorder
stories.standfirst: Amazon says its Bee Frontier listens all day for $74.99, with seven days of battery, and a $11.99-a-month Bee Pro plan hooks it into Alexa and Amazon shopping.
body: Bee, the AI wearable startup Amazon bought in 2025, announced two devices on Thursday, TechCrunch reported. The Bee Frontier, at $74.99, is available now on Amazon. The Bee Eclipse, a credit-card-sized recorder that magnetically attaches to the back of a phone, costs $99.99 and follows soon after.

Amazon says the Frontier, worn on the wrist or pinned to clothing, is IP67 water resistant, has dual microphones and runs up to seven days on a charge. Both devices turn conversations into summaries, to-do lists and calendar invites, and an indicator light shows when one is summarising. The Verge noted the new device can now help users buy things.

Free use covers conversation summaries with 14 days of memory. A Bee Pro subscription at $11.99 a month adds unlimited summaries, Amazon.com and Alexa+ integrations, suggested to-dos and a chat assistant. With Alexa connected, Amazon says Voice ID spots when the owner is speaking and records conversations for Bee's insights.

On privacy, Amazon says raw audio is processed in real time and deleted, and that transcripts are encrypted with keys the device controls, so no one at Amazon can read them unless users share them. Those are the company's claims; no independent testing has been published. TechCrunch lists rivals Plaud Note at $159 and Pocket at $129.

stories.headline: Anthropic tells investors distillation brings in 5 to 7 percent of revenue
stories.standfirst: The Decoder, citing The Information and the Financial Times, says Anthropic expects that income to fall, and that some investors now see an IPO valuation under $1.5 trillion.
body: Anthropic estimates that 5 to 7 percent of its revenue comes from distillation, where other companies use its models to train their own, according to The Decoder. The outlet cites The Information and the Financial Times, which in turn cite investor meetings in San Francisco. Anthropic has not published these figures, and this paper has not seen the investor materials.

The Decoder reports that Anthropic told investors the distillation income is likely to fall, weighing on the current quarter. The company is said to expect that blocking the practice will help in the long run, because it would make it harder for rivals to match the quality of Claude. How Anthropic would block it was not described in the report.

The same article puts third-quarter revenue at $16.8 billion, up roughly 45 percent from the second quarter, against a rise of more than 140 percent the quarter before. The Decoder attributes part of the slowdown to a summer lull and to OpenAI's September launch of Astra, and says Anthropic answered in late September with Opus 5.5.

On profit, The Decoder says The Information reports an adjusted operating margin of 11 percent for the year through the third quarter, excluding costs such as stock-based compensation. It says the Financial Times calls this the second straight quarter of adjusted profit, and that Anthropic is said to be cash-flow positive. Anthropic earned $1.70 in revenue for each dollar spent on compute.

The listing is planned for November, before Thanksgiving, per The Information. Anthropic's private valuation was $965 billion in May, and some bankers had floated $2 trillion for the IPO. The Decoder says some investors found the numbers disappointing and expect advisers to lower the target, possibly under $1.5 trillion. Anthropic has not commented in anything seen here, and the valuation talk is relayed from others.

stories.headline: Fish Audio's Drama 3 voice model now runs in vLLM-Omni
stories.standfirst: The 35-billion-parameter speech model activates 3 billion per token and speaks 83 languages, its model card says, and vLLM reports 255 ms to first audio.
body: Fish Audio has published Drama 3, a text-to-speech model built for multi-character scenes and long-form audio, and the vLLM project said on Thursday that its vLLM-Omni server now supports it. According to the model card, it has about 35 billion parameters in total, with 3 billion active for each token, and covers 83 languages.

The card says a single script can carry up to 16 speakers, marked with tags from speaker 0 to speaker 15, and that voices can be cloned from a reference clip and its transcript. Inline tags add sighs and laughs, and earlier takes can be fed back as context to edit a performance. Fish Audio also says long text is split into chunks automatically, with optional streaming.

The speed figures come from the makers. The model card claims a median 88.9 ms to first audio for one stream on an Nvidia H200. The vLLM post says its merged optimisation reaches 128 concurrent streams on one H200, with 255 ms median time to first audio and 222.2 seconds of audio generated per second, averaged over five runs of 1,088 English Seed-TTS-Eval requests.

To try it, vLLM gives the command vllm serve fishaudio/drama-3 --omni --port 8091 on current upstream code, and says it streams 44.1 kHz audio through its speech endpoint. One snag: the model card links a community licence while its metadata lists a research licence, so anyone planning commercial use should check the licence file. No independent tests of quality or speed have been published yet.

stories.headline: Player-1 agents learn to play games from 16 synthetic worlds
stories.standfirst: Two Qwen3.5-based models rose from 10.5% to 38.3% on a Minecraft test after reinforcement learning, the paper's authors say, and also played Doom.
body: Researchers from the National University of Singapore, Tencent's ARC Lab and Nanyang Technological University have posted Player-1, a method for teaching computer-use agents to play video games. The paper had 121 upvotes on Hugging Face's daily papers page when read on Thursday morning.

The authors, according to the paper, add relative mouse movement, held keys and composite actions that press several inputs at once. They start with 6,044 curated gameplay trajectories, then run reinforcement learning across Player-1-Gym, sixteen made-up 2D and 3D environments. Tasks include aiming, combat, driving and menus.

The paper reports two models: Player-1-9B, built on Qwen3.5-9B, and Player-1-35B-A3B, built on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. The authors say the smaller one climbs from 10.54% to 38.33% on MineDojo-300, against 12.63% for the strongest baseline. On ViZDoom-10 the larger model scores 0.7236 against 0.3938 for GameWAM.

Gains on browser games were smaller, from 31.43% to 34.45%, and the Watch Dogs 2 example is a single run. The text read here does not say whether code, models or data will be released. Nobody outside the team appears to have reproduced the results yet.

stories.headline: TSMC guides fourth-quarter revenue up to $54.3 billion
stories.standfirst: The chipmaker's results page shows $46.72 billion in third-quarter revenue against a $44.6 billion to $45.8 billion forecast, with a $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion range for the next quarter.
body: TSMC reported third-quarter net revenue of US$46.72 billion on Thursday. That beat the US$44.6 billion to US$45.8 billion range it had guided, according to the quarterly results table on its investor page. The foundry makes most leading AI accelerators, so the gap between forecast and result is closely watched.

The table lists a gross margin of 66.4% and an operating margin of 58.7%. The operating margin is above the 56.0% to 58.0% range TSMC gave. Its guidance assumes 31.98 Taiwan dollars to the US dollar. The page as retrieved carries no net income, capital spending or management comment on AI demand.

For the fourth quarter, the table gives net revenue of US$52.3 billion to US$54.3 billion. It also gives a gross margin of 65.0% to 67.0% and an operating margin of 56.5% to 58.5%, on an exchange rate of 31.8. The page does not say how much comes from AI chips. These are guidance, not results.

Coverage Techmeme points to from CNBC says net income rose about 69% to a record for the sixth straight quarter on AI demand. We could not open that report or TSMC's full earnings release, so the profit figures are unverified here. The investor page itself attributes no growth rate to AI.

stories.headline: Figma lets teams write design rules in Markdown for AI agents
stories.standfirst: Figma Specs is a Markdown editor for design rules, and the company's code layers feature enters public beta, TechCrunch reported from Figma's first Config event in India.
body: Figma announced features on Wednesday to control how AI agents work in its design platform, according to TechCrunch, which reported from the company's first Config conference in India. The headline item is Figma Specs, a Markdown-based editor where a team writes down its design language. TechCrunch is the only account we have read so far.

Per the report, Specs can be a standalone Figma file or sit on the canvas. They can reference canvas elements and embed FigJam diagrams, code layers and designs. Figma says teams and agents can use a Spec as a reference while designing. Teams can also gather libraries and guidelines in one place that agents consult, which Figma says should make AI output more predictable.

Code layers add code to canvas designs for more interactive prototypes. They move to public beta after a private beta that began in June, TechCrunch said. Users can ask the agent to turn a design into code. Figma's MCP server now supports more than 20 new tools, including Open Code, Dia, Grok Bot and Sarvam, the report said.

Figma chief design officer Loredana Crisan told TechCrunch that 17 times more lines of code are produced today than in the past. Releases have grown only 1.3 times, she said, and much of that code is made to discover what a product should be. The report gives no date or pricing for Specs. It says the agent on canvas reached more users the week before.

stories.headline: Musk says SpaceX will repay Grok Bot users for errors
stories.standfirst: Elon Musk posted that SpaceX will "make you whole" if Grok Bot botches a purchase or leaks a card, adding it has never happened. No written policy backs the pledge.
body: Elon Musk said on X on Thursday that SpaceX will "make you whole" if Grok Bot makes a mistake with a purchase or leaks a user's card. In the same post he wrote that this has never happened yet. The post drew 464 likes and 149 replies when the paper read it, and he gave no amount, process or limit.

An earlier Musk post, about 30 minutes before, told users to ask Grok Bot to buy what they want elsewhere and get a better deal. He wrote that there are far more purchasing websites than Amazon. Neither post says which stores the bot supports, what it asks users to approve, or what plan is required.

The pledge appears to repeat one he made in August. Magica, a news site, reported on 27 August that Musk told an X user weighing bank-account access: "Try it out. If Grok Bot messes up, we will make you whole." The site called that a personal assurance rather than a published reimbursement programme.

Magica also reported that the consumer terms make users responsible for agent actions and generally cap the company's liability at the greater of fees paid or $100, except for gross negligence or wilful misconduct. It did not establish how the pledge relates to those terms, and SpaceX has not published a written policy on repayment that the paper could find.

Magica quoted a security researcher, Rasa Jurgutyte, who warned that an agent could misread a request or be manipulated through prompt injection. The paper could not confirm Musk's claim that no card has leaked. Grok Bot launched in beta on 11 August, according to Magica.

stories.headline: OpenAI agrees to stop using alleged Apple trade secrets in lawsuit
stories.standfirst: At a hearing, OpenAI agreed not to use material Apple says was stolen and to image the devices of 14 employees, and the judge called an injunction for Apple likely.
body: OpenAI agreed on Wednesday not to use trade secrets that Apple claims were stolen by employees who moved to OpenAI, while the companies' legal fight plays out. Bloomberg reported the commitment from a hearing, and 9to5Mac, citing Bloomberg, gave the details. The agreement is voluntary, and it follows Apple's request for a preliminary injunction.

OpenAI also committed to collect forensic images of devices belonging to 14 employees who may hold Apple's confidential information, 9to5Mac reported. Judge Edward Davila can enforce the agreement and could impose sanctions if OpenAI does not comply. He is also reported to have said he was likely to grant Apple's injunction request.

Davila called Apple's request to inspect every device and repository that might hold its secrets a huge ask. Apple's lawyer, John Desmarais, said Apple would confine inspections to a small group of former staff, saying OpenAI has a few bad apples rather than 400. Apple's suit names two former employees, Chang Liu and Tang Tan, as well as OpenAI and io Products.

OpenAI went on the offensive the same day. In a filing, it alleged that a former employee who left to return to Apple took more than 100 confidential files about unreleased hardware to personal accounts. International Cyber Digest relayed the claim, and Apple denies the allegations. The filing is OpenAI's account and has not been tested in court.

The case sits on the hardware side of the AI race. According to 9to5Mac, the court granted many of Apple's requests for expedited discovery on Tuesday, covering internal documents, forensic evidence and employee testimony. Neither article names the next hearing date, and 9to5Mac's report carries no on-the-record statement from OpenAI.

stories.headline: Vals AI says no model reached 2 out of 100 on its humanoid tasks
stories.standfirst: In real-time MuJoCo simulations, Vals says GPT-6.1 Sol averaged 51 on 13 robot-arm tasks, while the 11 humanoid tasks, which need balance and walking, stayed near zero.
body: Vals AI, which runs model evaluations, posted a robotics benchmark on Wednesday that puts frontier models in real-time MuJoCo physics simulations of a robot arm and a humanoid. Models receive only camera feeds and sensor readings and answer with motor commands. Vals says it tested them on 24 tasks built around spatial reasoning and reaction time, and says it is the first team to test a humanoid.

By Vals's account, every model did better on the arm. GPT-6.1 Sol averaged 51 out of 100 on the 13 arm tasks. On the 11 humanoid tasks, where the model has to balance and walk on its own, no model reached 2 out of 100. Vals posted the results in a thread and pointed to a methodology page, which this paper has not opened.

The simulations run in real time, so thinking time costs the model. Vals says GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol moved the robot in every episode, after 75 to 80 seconds on average. Every other model averaged more than two minutes before its first command, it says, and Grok 4.7 and Gemini 4 Argon never moved the robot in most episodes.

Vals says it simulated the 7-DoF Franka Emika Panda arm in MuJoCo and held it to the real arm's limits, from datasheet joint speeds to protective stops. The firm argues that such tests are only as good as the infrastructure behind them. A simulation is not a physical robot, so how the numbers carry over to hardware is not established.

Artificial Analysis launched a separate robot-arm benchmark the same evening, in which OpenAI's GPT models also lead. Both sets of results are the testers' own, and neither has been reproduced by an outside group. Vals's thread includes an animated clip of the simulated robots at work.

stories.headline: Anthropic tells investors third-quarter revenue reached $16.8 billion
stories.standfirst: Bloomberg reports the figure, up from about $11.6 billion in the second quarter, went to prospective investors as the company pushes ahead with plans to go public.
body: Anthropic told prospective investors that its revenue in the third quarter reached $16.8 billion, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with the matter. Bloomberg said the artificial intelligence company is pushing ahead with plans to go public. Anthropic has not published the figure itself, and this paper has not seen the investor materials.

Andrew Curran, who covers AI companies on X, posted numbers after what he described as a meeting that had just ended, saying people who attended had begun to report them. He wrote that third-quarter revenue rose 45% to $16.8 billion, from $11.6 billion in the second quarter and $4.7 billion in the first. His account is secondhand and names no source.

The arithmetic fits, since $16.8 billion is about 45% above $11.6 billion. A summary of a Financial Times report gives the second quarter as $11.5 billion and says Anthropic also told investors it was profitable on an adjusted basis in the third quarter. The Financial Times article could not be opened here, so the profit detail is unconfirmed.

Bloomberg reported earlier that preliminary second-quarter revenue was above $11.5 billion. Some social posts also quote a valuation near $965 billion and a November listing. No source this paper opened confirms a valuation, and one summary of Financial Times reporting says senior executives have not set a target. Another summary of a Wall Street Journal report says the listing slipped from October to November.

Those listing details could change, and Anthropic has not commented in anything seen here. What is reported so far is a set of figures given to investors, relayed by one news outlet and one commentator, with a second outlet's account in summary. The company's own filings, if it files publicly, would be the first place to check the numbers.

stories.headline: Nvidia says tuning lifted a chip-design agent's score from 55% to 95%
stories.standfirst: In a case study with Siemens' Fuse EDA agent, Nvidia says better skills and tool descriptions cut agent turns by two thirds, using Claude Opus 4.8 in Claude Code.
body: Nvidia published a developer blog post on Wednesday describing how it used NeMo Gym, its open library for evaluating and improving models and agents with environments, on an agent that automates standard-cell characterization in chip design. That step generates the timing, power and noise models for logic cells. The post is Nvidia's own account of its own tool.

The agent is Siemens' Fuse EDA AI Agent, which drives tools from the Solido Characterization Suite through MCP servers and skills and produces Liberty files. Nvidia's verifier rewards the output through five checks: coverage, validity, relative validation, accuracy and integrity. If any gate fails, the reward is zero, and accuracy is the fraction of values within tolerance.

The test used the open-source GF180MCU process design kit, with 229 standard cells across 36 process, voltage and temperature corners. Tuning runs covered two cells across all 36 corners. Nvidia says it ran about 25 rollouts, each taking roughly 1.5 to 2 hours. The model and harness stayed fixed throughout: Claude Opus 4.8, running in Claude Code.

Nvidia reports that the composite benchmark score rose from about 55% to about 95%. Average agent turns fell from 155 to 53, and average output tokens fell from about 81,000 to about 29,000, roughly 64% fewer. The authors credit refined characterization skills and tool descriptions, simpler overlapping file and shell interfaces, and tool inputs defined with explicit JSON schemas.

The authors say the approach of grading final artifacts, building domain-specific verifiers and running many rollouts could apply to other engineering agents, including those in electronic design automation and computer-aided engineering. That is a claim for the method, tested here on one task with one model. No independent group has repeated the numbers, and the benchmark is built and graded by Nvidia.

stories.headline: vLLM adaptive verification now works with draft models lacking a confidence head
stories.standfirst: A new estimator learns acceptance odds while serving, so EAGLE, MTP and DFlash checkpoints can use the feature with no retraining, the vLLM team says.
body: The vLLM project said on Wednesday that adaptive verification, a speculative-decoding feature that needed a drafter with a trained confidence head, now works with the draft models people already serve. According to the team's announcement and blog post, it is on the main branch behind a flag. The team lists MTP, EAGLE, DFlash and DSpark checkpoints without a head.

In speculative decoding a small draft model proposes tokens and the target model checks them. The blog says adaptive verification trims draft tokens with low predicted acceptance before the target's forward pass, which saves compute, and helps most at large batch sizes where the GPU is compute-bound. Until now it worked only with DSpark drafters, which ship with a trained head.

The fix is an online-fitted estimator, a logistic regression over the log-odds of the drafter's top token, with one shared slope and one intercept per draft position. It refits during serving from the target model's accept and reject decisions. The team says the top-token probability ranks drafts about as well as a trained head but overestimates acceptance, and the fit corrects that.

On DeepSeek-V4-Flash with DSpark, the post reports the estimator scored an AUC of 0.8336 against 0.8191 for the trained head, with a worse calibration error of 0.0100 against 0.0052. For MiMo-V2.5-Pro-FP4 with DFlash, it says adaptive verification stays on the throughput-interactivity frontier at five of seven concurrency levels. Most throughput gains appear in charts rather than stated numbers.

To use it, set enable_adaptive_verification to true in the speculative config, with probabilistic draft sampling. It needs an attention backend that supports variable-length verification, and the blog says MTP and EAGLE gain less than DFlash and DSpark. Giancarlo Delfin of Inferact built it, as PR 52228. The benchmarks are the project's own and have not been independently run.
